summary:
Yukon's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination, as do the human rights statutes of every other province and territory. Legal change of gender is available in Yukon as elsewhere in Canada, with birth certificates and other vital-statistics documents falling under territorial jurisdiction; the sources reviewed do not set out Yukon's own requirements for amending a marker.

The Yukon Legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March 2026, with members rising to speak across party lines. Yukon Party MLA Wade Istchenko (Kluane) praised the courage, resilience, contributions and accomplishments of transgender, two-spirited and gender-diverse Yukoners and said too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment and hate for too long. He cited a national study finding that transgender 15-17-year-olds face 7.6 times the risk of a suicide attempt. The tribute is Yukon's own cross-party, in-legislature acknowledgement of trans residents.

In June 2024 a Pride flag was allegedly vandalised and stolen from Holy Family Elementary School in Whitehorse's Porter Creek neighbourhood over a weekend, and a replacement flag was put up promptly. In a statement issued 12 June, Yukon Education Minister Jeanie McLean reaffirmed her commitment to Yukon's sexual orientation and gender identity policy (SOGI 123) and said Pride month celebrates the diversity that makes Yukon vibrant and strong.
tangentialFactors:
Both Yukon items in the sources are official statements rather than enforcement actions: a cross-party tribute in the legislature, and an education minister's statement after a Pride flag was taken from a religious elementary school in the capital. No police hate-crime classification, arrest or charge is reported in connection with the flag theft.

The suicide-attempt figure cited during the tribute is a national study result, not a Yukon measurement, and the national hate-crime series does not disaggregate to Yukon, so no Yukon-specific rate can be set against other jurisdictions.
localsOnly:
Yukon schools operate under the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity policy, SOGI 123, which the education minister publicly reaffirmed in June 2024.

Adoption by same-sex couples became lawful in Yukon in 2003, part of nationwide legalisation completed across all jurisdictions by 2011.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Yukon-level hate-crime or victimisation figures appear in the sources reviewed. The national police-reported series and Egale Canada's analysis are national aggregates; reported hate-crime rates are markedly higher in large metropolitan areas than in smaller communities and reporting infrastructure is thinner in sparsely populated areas, so a low reported count for Yukon would not establish low incidence.

Yukon's own requirements for changing a gender marker on a birth certificate or other vital-statistics document are not set out in the sources reviewed; the sources record only that legal gender change is available in every province and territory under varying rules.

No provision specific to Yukon on access to sex-segregated facilities or on gender-affirming care appears in the sources reviewed; the absence of such material is a gap in sourcing, not evidence that no rule exists.
